title: On the fraction wall, does one half end where three sixths ends?
description: A fraction wall shows one whole cut into halves, thirds, fourths, fifths and sixths, one row each. One half and three sixths are read off the wall and the video asks why they end at the same place, while Keeko doubts that fractions with different numbers can be equal.
teaching_notes: One idea: on a fraction wall, equal lengths line up from the same left end, and six sixths make the whole just as two halves do. Watch for students who think different numbers must mean different lengths.

source: Look at a fraction wall where 1 unit is split into halves, t
video_script.why: The child reads one half and three sixths off a fraction wall and sees why they have the same length.
video_script.substitution: none: the book's own fraction wall with rows of halves, thirds, fourths, fifths and sixths
video_script.anchor: the fraction wall of the book: one whole and rows of equal pieces
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says one half and three sixths cannot be the same length because they have different numbers. The numbers do not give the length of the pieces; reading both on the wall shows where each ends.
video_script.payoff_line: One half and three sixths are equal in length

final_answer.spoken: yes, the two lengths are equal

video_script.fraction_reading: one half, three sixths, one sixth, six sixths
maths_rules: fraction wall: 1 whole, then rows of halves, thirds, fourths, fifths and sixths, all lined up from the same left end
1/2 is the first piece of the row of halves and ends at the middle of the whole
3/6 is three pieces of 1/6 from the left end and ends at the same middle
6 pieces of 1/6 make 1 whole and 2 pieces of 1/2 make 1 whole
1/2 is half of the whole, so it is half of 6 sixths: 6 divided by 2 = 3, so 1/2 = 3/6
slip: Keeko thinks different numbers mean different lengths
video_script.design: One idea: read the two lengths off the same wall. The wall stays on screen; a vertical guide line runs down from the end of one half.
